title: Musicians' pay versus ordinary wages
summary: Musicians earned $100 a week in 1935 against $25-30; $120 on staff in 1943.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: I was just thinking about the economy of music, and what are your ideas about this? Now, I can remember in 1935, the average musician made $100.00 a week.
That was good money. But the average person on the street made $25 or $30.
My father's salary, top salary, was
I know. So that means we were making like two-thirds more than the average person.

Yeah. That was in the 1930s. Here it is the '70s and we aren't anywhere near -- if the average person makes $200 a week now, the average musician should be making at least $1,800.00 a week, which really doesn't hold true.

When I left NBC, the last two years there our salary was raised to $320.00, and that was the year the garbage collectors were raised to $315.00 with four weeks off in the summer, hospital benefits and the whole works. That shows you more or less what our position in the economy is. When I went on staff in 1943 the basic pay was $120.00 a week. And with overtime, generally my check ran over $200.00 for those two years, with overtime. Where the working man's salary, I think at that time, the equivalent of my father was a laborer on the railroad, went up to about $65.00, $70.00. So the musicians were still making three times what unskilled labor made. I guess you'd put it on the terms that a musician would be very skilled labor and, you know, physical labor jobs would be more or less unskilled in that you didn't have to spend 15 years learning how to do it.
Well, how do you think we got in the

position where prestigewise and financewise, we're just not up to what we should be, or what I think it should be. I realize that we're still better off than musicians in other countries, that's understood --

Well, yes, we are better off, say, than in Paris. I know there's a trombone player, he has to have -- he's got a staff job, he also works a nightclub and he works in the Opera Comique and he has to work three jobs to make a living, and he doesn't live in too good a place, besides. So that's true.

On the other hand, there's a lot more work in foreign countries. I think the Soviet Union comparatively, probably the musicians are best off. They're the ones that own the motorboats and the automobiles and everything.
Yeah, they're in a favored -- artists, scientists are fairly well off. But then, of course, to enjoy that you have to live in the Soviet Union, so --
